mcqs.question: In an undirected graph, DFS visits node v from node u, and v's neighbor list includes u (since the edge is stored both ways). Should this be flagged as a cycle?
options: Yes, since u has already been visited
Yes, but only if u has more than one neighbor
It depends on the order neighbors are stored in the adjacency list
No — u is v's parent in the DFS, so seeing it again is just the edge doubling back, not a cycle
mcqs.explanation: Because undirected edges are stored in both directions, the node you just arrived from will always appear as an already-visited neighbor — that's expected and not a cycle. A real cycle is signaled only by a visited neighbor that is NOT the immediate parent, meaning a second, different path back to an already-seen node.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't a plain 'has this node been visited anywhere before' check work for detecting cycles in a DIRECTED graph?
options: Directed graphs cannot contain cycles by definition
It flags false cycles on any node reachable via two separate, unrelated paths — a node fully finished on one branch can be legitimately revisited from a different branch with no cycle involved
Visited checks only work correctly on trees, not general directed graphs
Directed graphs never have more than one path to any node
mcqs.explanation: A DAG can easily have a node reachable via two independent, non-overlapping paths, and revisiting it from the second path is completely valid — a plain visited check can't distinguish that from an actual cycle, since it doesn't track whether the earlier visit is still in progress or already finished. Directed graphs absolutely can contain cycles, and having multiple paths to a node is common, not exceptional.

mcqs.question: In the three-color DFS cycle check, encountering a neighbor colored BLACK during the traversal means what?
options: A cycle has definitely been found
The neighbor is fully finished, from an already-explored, unrelated part of the graph — not a cycle
The neighbor is currently on the recursion stack
The neighbor has not been visited yet
mcqs.explanation: BLACK specifically means a node and all its descendants have been completely explored — encountering it means you've reached an already-finished, separate part of the graph, which is normal and not a cycle. A cycle is signaled only by encountering a GRAY node — one still actively on the current recursion path.

mcqs.question: Can Union-Find be used to detect cycles in a DIRECTED graph the same way it detects them in an undirected one?
options: Yes, with no modification needed
Yes, but only if the graph has fewer than V-1 edges
No — Union-Find has no notion of edge direction, so it can't distinguish a directed back edge (a cycle) from a directed cross edge (not a cycle)
No, because Union-Find only works on trees, not general graphs
mcqs.explanation: Union-Find's same-set check works because undirected edges have no direction to track — but a directed graph can have two nodes in the same weakly-connected set with no actual directed cycle between them, which Union-Find cannot distinguish. It has nothing to do with edge count, and it works on general graphs, just undirected ones specifically for this purpose.

mcqs.question: You're checking for cycles in an undirected graph as edges are added one at a time over a long-running process, with frequent 'has a cycle formed yet?' queries. Which approach fits best?
options: Union-Find, since it answers each incremental check in near-O(1) amortized time without re-traversing the whole graph
Parent-tracking DFS, re-run from scratch after every single edge addition
Neither approach can handle incrementally arriving edges
The three-color method, since it's the only one that detects cycles at all
mcqs.explanation: Union-Find is built exactly for this online scenario — each edge addition is a same-set check plus a union, both near-O(1) amortized, with no need to re-traverse anything. Re-running DFS after every edge would work but cost O(V+E) per addition, and the three-color method is specifically for directed graphs, not the mechanism of choice here.

mcqs.question: Someone applies the undirected graph's 'skip the parent' cycle-detection rule directly to a directed graph. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing — the rule generalizes cleanly to directed graphs with no changes needed
Directed edges don't double back the way undirected ones do, so there's no parent edge to skip, and the rule doesn't correctly identify real cycles in a directed graph
The code will fail to compile due to a type mismatch
The rule works but runs slower on directed graphs
mcqs.explanation: The parent-skipping trick exists specifically because undirected edges are stored bidirectionally, creating an artificial 'revisit' of the node you just came from — directed edges have no such doubling-back, so there's nothing analogous to skip, and the rule simply doesn't map onto what makes a directed cycle. This is a correctness issue, not a performance or compilation one.
